business_model.basis: stated directly in the 10-K Item 1 Business description
business_model.claim: Mastercard is a technology company in the global payments industry that operates a proprietary network to switch (authorize, clear and settle) payment transactions across more than 220 countries and territories.
quotes: Mastercard is a technology company in the global payments industry.

We operate a payments network that provides choice and flexibility for consumers, merchants and our customers. Through our unique and proprietary global payments network, we switch (authorize, clear and settle) payment transactions.

business_model.claim: Mastercard does not issue cards, extend credit, or earn revenue from interest rates; it connects consumers, financial institutions, merchants, governments, digital partners and businesses.
quotes: We do not issue cards, extend credit, determine or receive revenue from interest rates or other fees charged to account holders by issuers, nor do we establish the rates charged by acquirers in connection with merchants' acceptance of our products.

competitive_position.basis: Stated in the 10-K Item 1 Business strategy section.
competitive_position.claim: Mastercard's strategy rests on three interdependent priorities—consumer payments, commercial and new payment flows, and services and other solutions—enabled by people, brand, data and AI, technology, franchise, and doing well by doing good.
quotes: Our strategy centers on growing our core, diversifying our customers and geographies and building new areas for the future through a combination of organic and inorganic strategic initiatives.
Our priorities strengthen, complement and reinforce each other and are fundamentally interdependent.

competitive_position.basis: Stated in the 10-K Risk Factors under Competition and Technology.
competitive_position.claim: Mastercard faces competition from general purpose payments networks, debit and local networks, ACH and real-time account-based payments systems, digital wallets, fintechs, digital public infrastructure, government-backed solutions, and digital currencies.
quotes: We compete against general purpose payments networks, debit and local networks, ACH and real-time account-based payments systems, digital wallets and other fintechs (focused on online activity across various channels and processing payments using in-house capabilities), digital public infrastructure and other government-backed solutions and digital currencies.

competitive_position.basis: Stated in the 10-K Risk Factors under Business and Operations.
competitive_position.claim: Disintermediation risk exists from merchants and third-party processors switching transactions directly with issuers, from fintechs developing platforms that bypass Mastercard, and from central banks experimenting with CBDCs that could reduce Mastercard's role.
quotes: Parties that process our transactions in certain countries (such as merchants and third-party payment processors) may try to eliminate our position as an intermediary in the payment process by switching transactions directly with issuers or processing transactions directly between issuers and acquirers.

Fintechs and technology companies could develop platforms or networks that disintermediate us from digital payments as well as develop products or services that compete with our customers and could diminish demand for our products and services.

competitive_position.basis: Stated in the 10-K Risk Factors under Payments Industry Regulation.
competitive_position.claim: Regulatory action on interchange rates, no-surcharge rules, and network fees could materially reduce transaction volumes and profitability.
quotes: If we are ultimately unsuccessful in defending our ability to establish interchange rates, any resulting legislation, regulation and/or litigation may have a material adverse impact on our overall business and results of operations.
If, over time, an increased number of merchants choose to surcharge as permitted, this could result in consumers viewing our products less favorably and/or using alternative means of payment.

competitive_position.basis: Stated in the 10-K Risk Factors under Preferential or Protective Government Actions.
competitive_position.claim: Preferential or protective government actions, including mandates for domestic switching, data localization requirements, foreign ownership restrictions, and growth of local payment networks, could restrict Mastercard's ability to operate in particular geographies.
quotes: Governments in some countries have implemented, or may implement, regulatory requirements that mandate switching of domestic payments either entirely in that country or by only domestic companies.

Governments have been increasingly creating and expanding local payments structures, which are increasingly being considered as alternatives to traditional domestic payment solutions and schemes such as ours.

competitive_position.basis: Stated in the 10-K Risk Factors under Privacy, Data, AI and Information Security.
competitive_position.claim: Increasingly complex and fragmented privacy, data, AI, and information security regulations across jurisdictions may increase compliance costs, restrict data use, and expose Mastercard to fines and enforcement actions.
quotes: We are subject to increasingly complex, fragmented, overlapping and/or divergent laws and regulations related to privacy and data protection, data use and governance, AI and information security (including with respect to cybersecurity and cyber-risk) in the jurisdictions in which we do business.

competitive_position.basis: Stated in the 10-K Risk Factors under Litigation.
competitive_position.claim: Mastercard is a defendant in civil litigations and regulatory proceedings including antitrust and intellectual property claims, and certain limitations have already been placed on its business through litigation settlements.
quotes: We are a defendant in a number of civil litigations and regulatory proceedings and investigations, including among others, those alleging violations of competition and antitrust law and those involving intellectual property claims.
Certain limitations have been placed on our business because of litigation and litigation settlements, such as changes to our no-surcharge rule in the U.S. and Canada.

growth_thesis.basis: Stated in P6 (earnings release bullet) and P1 (10-K strategy and performance table); the cash-displacement framing is management's stated strategy, not an independent forecast.
growth_thesis.claim: Core payment network gross dollar volume (GDV) growth is a primary revenue driver: Q3 2026 GDV rose 7% and purchase volume 9% on a local-currency basis, and full-year 2025 GDV reached $10.6T, up 9% locally. For this to continue, global consumer and merchant spending on electronic payments must keep expanding and the secular shift away from physical cash must persist.
quotes: Third quarter gross dollar volume up 7% and purchase volume up 9%, on a local currency basis
Capturing the significant secular opportunity of cash displacement by increasing acceptance through advancing technology and partnering with players across the payments ecosystem

growth_thesis.basis: Growth figures stated in P6 and P1; the risk of restriction is stated in P2 (10-K Risk Factors).
growth_thesis.claim: Cross-border transaction volume is a distinct growth engine: Q3 2026 cross-border volume grew 11% on a local-currency basis (9 months up 12%), and full-year 2025 cross-border volume grew 15% locally. For this to continue, international trade and travel flows must remain resilient and no new jurisdictional barriers (data-localisation mandates, trade sanctions, or restrictions on cross-border switching) must materially restrict Mastercard's ability to switch transactions across borders.
quotes: up 7% | up 11% | up 9%
up 9% | up 10%
Regional groups of countries are considering, or may consider, efforts to restrict our switching of regional transactions.

growth_thesis.basis: Stated in P3 (10-K MD&A net-revenue table and narrative) and P1 (10-K Business section describing the service portfolio).
growth_thesis.claim: Value-added services and solutions (security, data, AI, authentication, processing, consumer engagement) is the fastest-growing revenue line: it rose 23% in 2025 to $13,315 (table in millions), or 21% currency-neutral. For this to continue, financial-institution and merchant customers must keep adopting and paying for these add-on solutions, and Mastercard must differentiate its data and AI offerings against competing technology providers.
quotes: Net revenue from our value-added services and solutions increased 23%, or 21% on a currency-neutral basis, in 2025 versus the prior year, which included a 3 percentage point increase from Acquisitions.

We offer security solutions, consumer acquisition and engagement, business and market insights, digital and authentication, processing and gateway and other solutions (including ACH batch and real-time account-based payments and solutions and open finance).

growth_thesis.basis: Transaction counts and growth rates stated in P6 and P1; the >70% switching share is stated in P1.
growth_thesis.claim: Switched-transaction count growth underpins transaction-processing assessments: Q3 2026 switched transactions grew 9% year-over-year, and full-year 2025 volume was 175.5B transactions, up 10%. For this to continue, the number of active credentials (cards, tokens, digital wallets) must keep growing and new payment rails (real-time, ACH, account-based) must add incremental switched transactions rather than merely shifting existing card volume.
quotes: up 7% | up 11% | up 9%
We switch more than 70% of all transactions for Mastercard and Maestro-branded cards, including nearly all cross-border transactions.
